title: A good worker
content:
The truth is, I’m not a good worker. I’ve had very few traditional jobs, and my performance on typical tasks was poor.

Work the exact hours, do precisely what’s asked, don’t ask questions and focus on what the boss wants.

We modeled ‘good worker’ behavior in school. “Will this be on the test?” was the key question for 100 years. Do what the teacher asks for, and don’t overthink it.

The indoctrination of compliance came from factory owners. It’s easier to run an industrial operation when you can treat your workers as interchangeable cogs, not individuals.

We took that idea to schools, to communities, and even to how some engaged in spirituality.

The good worker trope falls apart when the world changes fast. It becomes a hindrance when job security wavers. And it doesn’t really pay off when AI and the atomization of work mean that most of us are the boss now, even if we are on a payroll.

It’s better to be a good leader, a resilient contributor and someone who has the insight and guts to ask why.

title: First Case of Teeth Growing Out of an Eye Socket
content:
A 16-year-old boy in India has had a tooth removed from his left eye socket, between the eyelid and the eyebrow. He had noticed a painless swelling for about a month, but was only taken to hospital when two hard, whitish points began poking through. A scan revealed a fully formed canine tooth—an extremely unusual example of an ectopic tooth.

[Ectopic teeth](https://www.aaojournal.org/article/S0161-6420(25)00801-2/fulltext) are teeth that develop or erupt in the wrong place. Instead of following the usual path to the mouth, they end up somewhere else. They can be normal baby or adult teeth, or sometimes extra teeth known as supernumerary [teeth](https://theconversation.com/topics/teeth-2317).

Ectopic teeth are most often found in the maxillary sinus—the hollow space behind the cheekbone—but they have also been found in the nasal cavity, palate, chin, jaw joint and eye socket. A [review of 61 published cases](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10548160/) found that they can go unnoticed for years or cause pain, swelling, headaches or difficulty opening the mouth. A tooth growing inside the nose can lead to a blocked nose, discharge and nosebleeds.

So how does a tooth end up somewhere as strange as an eye socket?

The face develops from several groups of cells and tissues that move and join together in the womb. Tooth development depends on interactions between some of these tissues. If this process goes awry, a tooth can sometimes develop in an abnormal location—even away from the mouth.

Developmental problems are not the only possible explanation. A [review](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7920564/) of ectopic teeth in the upper jaw also lists injuries, dental treatment and growths such as cysts and tumours as possible causes.

Having several extra teeth can sometimes be a sign of an inherited condition. One example is [cleidocranial dysplasia](https://www.hopkinsmedicine.org/health/expert-qa/cleidocranial-dysplasia-ccd), a rare genetic disorder that affects the development of bones and teeth. Other [much rarer genetic conditions](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3188466/) have also been linked to extra teeth.

The Indian teenager had no history of trauma, and doctors could not determine why teeth had developed in his eye socket.

**How Are Ectopic Teeth Found and Treated?**

Whether an ectopic tooth needs removing depends on where it is and whether it is causing problems. An isolated tooth with no symptoms can sometimes just be monitored, but it may need to be removed if it causes an infection, blocks a passage, damages nearby structures or is linked to a cyst.

Doctors use scans to pinpoint the tooth and see what lies close to it. A CT scan can show whether it sits near the eyes, nerves or blood vessels, which helps them decide whether to operate.

Surgery ranges from a simple extraction to a complex operation. For teeth in the nose or sinuses, surgeons can often use an endoscope—a thin tube with a camera and surgical instruments on the end—to remove them through the nostrils rather than making a larger cut. A [review](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31277707/) identified 27 published cases in which ectopic teeth in the nose or sinuses were removed this way.

Before surgery, the most common symptoms were nasal obstruction, discharge, facial pain and nosebleeds. The review found that endoscopic removal worked in the reported cases, although the evidence comes from a handful of published cases rather than large clinical trials.

Removing an ectopic tooth does not mean another ordinary tooth will grow in its place. But people with one supernumerary tooth can sometimes have others, so doctors may use scans to look for them. A few reports describe another extra tooth developing in the same area after removal, although this appears to be extremely rare.

In the Indian teenager’s case, the scan found no other ectopic teeth. His tooth had simply ended up in a very unusual place. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)![Image 2](https://assets.nautil.us/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

Read the[original article](https://theconversation.com/first-case-of-teeth-growing-out-of-an-eye-socket-what-you-need-to-know-about-ectopic-teeth-293247)._

title: Even Dogs Seem to Experience the Mysterious Bouba/Kiki Effect
content:
The bouba/kiki effect is one of the odder psychological phenomena. For some reason, when presented with two random shapes (one angular and another rounded), and two nonsense words (“kiki” and “bouba”), people tend to associate bouba with the lobed figure and kiki with the spiky one. First discovered in the 1920s, this particular idiosyncrasy of the human mind is a strong indication that we associate certain sounds with certain shapes, which has important implications for the evolution of language.

Kiki and bouba, I think you can guess which is which. _Credit: Adobe Stock_

It’s also proved to be strikingly widespread. Cultures from around the globe speaking different languages can “correctly” identify bouba and kiki (including those with no written language). In fact, when people who have been blind since birth are presented with 3D representations of the figures, they too get it right. Now, according to a new study [published](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspb.2026.1209) in the _Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences_, the bouba/kiki effect may even extend to dogs.

To investigate the possibility of a canine bouba/kiki effect, a team of animal behaviorists recruited 51 dogs and their owners. They invited the pairs into a room with two screens on either wall, one of which displayed the rounded bouba figure and the other displaying the sharp kiki figure. After the dogs settled in, the team played a human voice saying the words “bouba” and “kiki” over a set of speakers while a camera recorded their reactions. In an effort to avoid the owners accidentally sending [subtle cues](https://nautil.us/how-a-psychic-horse-named-clever-hans-changed-the-way-we-do-science-1284622) to their canines, the researchers repeated the experiment with 19 dogs whose owners were wearing headphones.

**Read more: “**[**Why Do Some People Look Like Their Dogs?**](https://nautil.us/why-do-some-people-look-like-their-dogs-1175313)**”**

The team used artificial intelligence to track where and for how long the canines looked during the experiment. They found that the dogs tended to look longer at the rounded shape when the word “bouba” was played and longer at the angular shape more often when the word “kiki” was played. (Weird, right?)

It’s not the first time the bouba/kiki effect has been found in animals, however. A study [published](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.adq7188) earlier this year found that baby chickens, freshly hatched from their eggs, made the association. The chicks, however, showed an overall bias toward rounded shapes, and the researchers discovered something similar in this study.

Overall, dogs in the first setup showed a general bias toward gazing at the kiki shape. But this bias wasn’t present in the second setup, when the owners’ ears were covered. According to the team, this strange discrepancy probably can’t be chalked up to subtle cues. “It could be hypothesized that the dogs were influenced by the owners’ unintentional cues,” they write. “However, since humans typically show a stronger preference for rounded or curved shapes rather than spiky ones, this is unlikely.”

Instead, the bias toward spiky shapes in the larger, first experimental group may have something to do with a sensory bias in dogs. “In the case of dogs, animals’ facial configuration, especially when considering ancient dogs and wolves, is characterized by more angular, ‘spiky’ features, which contrasts with the round facial morphology typical of human infants and could plausibly contribute to an opposite bias,” they wrote.

In other words, dog morphology is relatively spiky so they prefer spiky shapes, whereas our faces are round so we prefer rounder shapes.

Of course, the researchers stress that all of this will take more study with larger sample sizes to suss out. But either way, welcome to the bouba/kiki club, canines! ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: This Fish Is the Kobayashi of the Sea
content:
While many of us were on vacation in July, marine biologists from [SpeSeas](https://speseas.org/team/) were hard at work peering at eelpouts, squat lobsters, and carnivorous sponges. Hosted aboard the Schmidt Ocean Institute’s ship _Falkor_, the research group [completed the most comprehensive deep-sea survey ever](https://schmidtocean.org/first-caribbean-led-expedition-to-explore-trinidad-and-tobagos-deep-sea-unveils-rich-ecosystems/) around the islands of Trinidad and Tobago, discovering 20 potential new species.

**Read more: “**[**Behold, Crawzilla, the Not-Quite-Biggest Crayfish Ever Caught**](https://nautil.us/behold-crawzilla-the-not-quite-biggest-crayfish-ever-caught-1285273)**”**

Along the way, though, they got a whole new look at previously recorded species as well. Case in point: An ROV cruising about 1,259 meters below the sea surface secured footage of a black swallower fish that had just consumed prey many times its body size. The species (_Chiasmodon niger_) grows to only about 4 to 8 inches long, yet [pursues fish as much as four times its length and 10 times its mass](https://twilightzone.whoi.edu/explore-the-otz/creature-features/black-swallower/). It can eat such fish whole by dislocating its jaw and distending its stomach like a balloon, leaving it looking like a snake that’s eaten a rabbit.

The black swallower wasn’t physically captured by the ROV, so the exact contents of its stomach can’t be diagnosed. “If only we had a CT scanner at sea,” lead author Diva Amon lamented in a [press release](https://www.sciencealert.com/a-little-fish-in-the-deep-sea-swallowed-a-meal-way-bigger-than-itself-scientists-caught-it-on-camera). “The mystery of what this little guy had for lunch may never be solved."

Still, with few exceptions, past sightings have only been of dead black swallowers, like the [one caught in 2007](https://www.reddit.com/r/natureismetal/comments/8dn996/black_swallower_died_trying_to_eat_a_fish_4_times/) by a fisherman in Grand Cayman that had eaten a huge snake mackerel. (Black swallowers are difficult to spot alive because they spend most of their time way down in the twilight zone.) If the diminutive predator gets too ambitious, it can’t digest the prey before decomposition starts, releasing gases that force the pair to the surface, where they both die. The Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution [compares the feeding behavior of the black swallower to a hot-dog eating contest](https://twilightzone.whoi.edu/explore-the-otz/creature-features/black-swallower/).

It’s an apt comparison as the black swallower filmed by the ROV was trying to swim with an extremely distended belly on which the skin had stretched so much that it was transparent, a window into the fish’s internal organs.

Talk about gorging yourself until you might burst. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: How Prehistoric People Survived After One of the Worst Volcanic Eruptions in History
content:
Around 5,250 BCE a series of volcanic activity rocked Japan’s southernmost island, Kyushu. Known as the Kikai-Akahoya eruption, the blast was enormous, notching a seven on the Volcanic Explosivity Index (which only goes up to eight), and causing waves of destruction that ravaged the greater archipelago.

“This eruption must have been devastating, exploding out of the seabed with little warning,” Lund University archaeologist Peter Jordan explained in a [statement](https://www.lunduniversity.lu.se/article/how-one-earths-worst-volcanic-disasters-affected-societies). “It battered the Japanese islands with powerful earthquakes and enormous tsunamis, and then blanketed the landscape with meters of volcanic ash.”

**Read more: “**[**A Blow‑by‑Blow Account of What Would Happen If the Yellowstone Supervolcano Erupted Now**](https://nautil.us/a-blow%E2%80%91by%E2%80%91blow-account-of-what-would-happen-if-the-yellowstone-supervolcano-erupted-now-1285322)**”**

How this apocalyptic event affected the Jomon, the dominant Japanese hunter-gatherer culture at the time, has been the subject of some debate. According to traditional views of the fallout, local groups were immediately annihilated and the area was eventually resettled, as evidenced by the layer of volcanic ash separating one disappearing style of pottery from another in the island’s archaeological record.

But after further investigation, another school of thought emerged. Some styles of pottery managed to survive—even on Kyushu. So the “Jomon survival” scenario arose as a counterweight to the “Jomo apocalypse” doomsayers. Now Jordan and his colleagues are out with a new [study](http://dx.doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aeh7197) in _Science Advances_, further complicating things.

To find out how the apocalyptic event affected population numbers throughout Japan, an international team of archaeologists turned to radiocarbon dating data. Using time-frequency of radiocarbon dates as a proxy for population (essentially, more stuff means a higher population), the team was able to apply statistical models to estimate population changes after the eruption.

Their findings point to a more nuanced scenario, somewhere in between annihilation and continuity. While Jomom population numbers dropped precipitously in the immediate area, they actually increased in nearby locales. The areas closest to ground zero had been in decline for some time, so the region was sparsely populated when the eruptions occurred. Additionally, populations near the northern coastline grew after the disaster, even though the countryside was ecologically destroyed (potentially because the marine ecosystem wasn’t hit as hard).

According to the team, these findings suggest refugees from the eruption managed to hold on, migrate, and continue their lives. “The disaster caused major loss of life,” study author Enrico Crema of Cambridge University said. “However, survivors migrated, forged new social relations, innovated new kinds of economy, and appear to have found creative ways to exist and later thrive in the new post-disaster conditions.”

The Kikai-Akahoya eruption was a devastating event in Japan’s prehistory, but it also tells a story of human resilience in the face of disaster. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Here’s How Freaky the Universe Would Look If Light Slowed to 3 Miles Per Hour
content:
Day to day, most of us don’t give much thought to the fundamental fact of physics that light is traveling across the universe at nearly 671 million miles per hour. But a new simulator asks a fun question: How would the universe appear if light moved at a much, much slower speed?

A new web project called [Relativity Park](https://rivendell.dmitrybrant.com/relativity/) from developer [Dmitry Brant](https://dmitrybrant.com/2026/09/13/relativity-park-taming-the-speed-of-light) lets us explore a world where the speed of light is set at 3.11 miles per hour, or a brisk walking pace. At this speed, the rules set down by Einstein’s 1905 theory of special relativity start to become much more obvious, with some mind-bending and eye-popping results.

In Relativity Park, light moves at a brisk walking pace. _Credit: Dmitry Brant_

To summarize his theory: The speed of light is fixed, no matter if you’re standing still or traveling close to the speed of light yourself. That means, as your own observing speed changes, the speed of light does not. Instead, time and space have to begin distorting themselves to compensate.

In reality, you’re never going to get anywhere close to the speed of light, whether you’re on a rocket launcher or strolling down the road, so these space and time warps are imperceptible (though astronauts on the ISS do age fractions of a second slower). Step into Relativity Park, however, and these distortions show up quite noticeably.

**Read more: “**[**5 Amazing New Discoveries About Light**](https://nautil.us/5-amazing-new-discoveries-about-light-353079)**”**

All the instructions you need are on screen, but try holding down the up arrow or the W key for a second or two. This speeds up your pace, getting closer to the (slow) speed of light. Everything in front of you bunches together (relativistic aberration) and gets shifted toward the color blue (Doppler color).

Speed up, and you’ll see distortions in space, time, and color. _Credit: Dmitry Brant_

Use the mouse to turn around, and the scenery is stretched out and redder, as this is away from your direction of travel—the same effects, but opposite.

Turn to look behind you, and light gets redder and darker. _Credit: Dmitry Brant_

You’ll also notice brighter colors ahead of you (light piling up) and darker colors behind you (light thinning out). Occasionally, an object will appear bright in a dark area, which is the counteraction of its own motion, relative to the speed of light.

Keep an eye on the stopwatch in the bottom right corner too, which shows time as you’re experiencing it, and the time in the world around you. Look at the flashing lampposts as well—their timing and color doesn’t change, but your perspective will as you speed up or slow down.

“The thing that continues to boggle my mind, and the thing that I appreciate even deeper after finishing this app, is how Einstein could have envisioned this geometry and all its implications from first principles, without the benefit of pretty visualizations,” [says](https://dmitrybrant.com/2026/09/13/relativity-park-taming-the-speed-of-light) Brant. “I hope this visualization can serve as a reminder of how weird our world actually is, at high enough speeds and high enough energies.” ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Why Story and Playtime Really Matter
content:
When baby needs watching and mom and dad get busy, the blue light of a glowing rectangle often beckons. Instead of playing another round of peek-a-boo while dinner burns, they may turn to a phone, iPad, or television to serve as a babysitter. Most babies now get screen time daily, according to recent [data](https://epi.org.uk/publications-and-research/babies-and-screentime/) from the United Kingdom, with the average hovering around 41 minutes a day for 9-month-olds.

What does this screen time do to their tender, developing brains? Infants are thought to learn best by doing, particularly when it comes to language and social skills. They rely heavily on face-to-face interaction, shared attention, and live conversational feedback with an adult caregiver, [decades](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0960982224003178) of [evidence](https://www.cell.com/current-biology/fulltext/S0960-9822(24)00317-8?_returnURL=https%3A%2F%2Flinkinghub.elsevier.com%2Fretrieve%2Fpii%2FS0960982224003178%3Fshowall%3Dtrue) suggests. Differences in social engagement abilities are also a major feature of autism spectrum disorder, and deficits in this arena have been associated with [slowed](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/aur.1624) language development.

**Read more:**[**“For Kids, Learning Is Moving”**](https://nautil.us/for-kids-learning-is-moving-236112)

To probe this question of how social interaction and screen time affect a baby’s brain, a trio of researchers from Northwestern University recently invited 49 pairs of parents and infants, aged 22 to 44 months, into the lab to play as they would at home, with a book or a puzzle or other toys. They then used electroencephalogram (EEG) headgear to compare the babies’ brain activity during natural play versus staring at a screen.

What the scientists found was that certain brain waves associated with attention, social engagement, and learning were more active when the baby was playing with a parent compared to when they were watching television, even together. The scientists found the same patterns in an independent sample of children diagnosed with autism. They published their [results](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bandl.2026.105848) this week in _Brain and Language_.

I spoke with study author Elizabeth Norton, professor of communication science and disorders, about what social engagement looks like in a baby, what it’s like to get an EEG cap on a baby, and whether the results suggest that screen time inhibits language development.

**The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends zero screen time for infants. Why is that?**

Research takes so long to do, and what we know about screen time has evolved so quickly. For very young kids, there’s still not a lot of great information about how being in front of a screen affects their brain development.

And even for older kids, the American Academy of Pediatrics says some screen time is okay. It’s ideal when parents and caregivers can use that time together, almost in the way that they would when they’re reading a book, to use it as a jumping off point for conversations and back and forth interactions.

One of the factors that makes the AAP conservative or conscientious in their recommendations for young kids is that we know how important those back-and-forth reciprocal relations with caregivers and adults are for infants under two years old. I believe that being extra careful to make sure that families prioritize those interactions as much as is feasible is part of the reason for that recommendation.

**And is all screen time created equal?**

It’s really about having someone next to you and using screen time as a way to engage in what we call joint attention. An example is that a child might be playing with a Lego tower, building something, and the child and the caregiver’s attention are shared back and forth around that object. We know that’s so important for language development and social development and a lot of other things.

When screen time can be something that is shared that can be really productive. But of course, some families might need to have kiddos watch a screen for a few minutes while mom takes a shower or dad cooks dinner. In the real world, screen time for short periods can be a real necessity, but it’s ideal when it’s not just the child getting all of their language input from screens.

**This study was presented as paradigm shifting because usually the social interaction and brain activity of babies are measured when they’re engaged in highly structured activities as opposed to more natural ones. Why had this approach not been tried before, and why is this shift so important?**

When we’ve studied young kids’ language development and social development, we traditionally bring them into the lab and do things that really don’t align with their everyday experiences. We make them listen to streams of unfamiliar voices out of disembodied speakers, or we put single black-and-white pictures of faces up on a screen.

Even though with this study, we had parents and kids come into our lab, where it’s more feasible for us to put an EEG cap on the kid—and then also the parent for some additional analysis that we’re doing in future work—what we did is let them play like they normally do. We gave them books or puzzles and said, “Play like you were at home.” And we looked at their brains during those moments and compared it to what was happening in their brains when they were watching a video with or without the parent.

The real innovation that gets me excited is that we used to try to induce states of language learning or social processing in kids. And the real flip that we implemented here is to let those states unfold naturally. That is one of the things that was exciting to me, especially with the second study we did, where we included a group of kids who were diagnosed with autism.

So many studies show that kids who are diagnosed as autistic have differences in the way they process faces or listen to language, but it might be due to experimental conditions. The push to take our neuroscience tools from the really rigid and experimental to the real world is really exciting, potentially transformative for understanding a lot of things, including autism.

**You found that social engagement in some of these activities went beyond eye contact. Is that correct?**

We didn’t measure just eye contact. What we were measuring, to characterize social engagement, was that the parent and the infant were going back and forth and taking turns and engaging. We were watching the videos of how they engaged. It’s not just that they were looking at each other, which they might have been, but it’s deeper than that in terms of having a conversation, essentially.

**Were there key elements of social interaction that you were looking for aside from eye contact?**

We adopted a framework that’s been used in previous studies to look at how a caregiver is responsive to their child’s behavior, which we know is really important for child development. We were looking for the stretches of the interaction where there was that back and forth of shared attention related to an object, a movie, a puzzle or a book.

**Do your findings suggest that screen time may inhibit language development?**

I would not go so far to say that screen time inhibits language development. This was a one-time study and so we want to be careful about talking about longitudinal consequences.

One of the things that this tells us is that there are signatures in the brain that we can identify from previous studies that indicate that the child is paying attention, they might be ready to learn, and we see those a lot more in the moments when they’re just engaging with their caregiver and not as much when they’re just engaging with a screen. We can’t necessarily say that screens are detrimental, but we do see patterns that are consistent with what we might want to see for learning when the child is going back and forth with their caregiver.

**You found that toddlers with slower language development and autism diagnoses showed similar brain patterns to children with typical development in the moments when they were engaged with the caregiver. Does this mean they are generally more engaged than we thought?**

It tells us that there are more universals in language development and language learning than we might have thought. And some of the differences that we’ve seen in previous studies, for example—which have found that groups of children who have been diagnosed with autism look at faces differently—might be related to the fact that these studies were not very natural. It’s not very often in our daily lives that we see a black and white representation of a face and think about how to engage with it.

**You plan to look next at whether parents and toddlers’ brains are in synchrony when they’re interacting. What will this tell you?**

The idea of looking at brain-to-brain synchrony is quite new. A few studies have done it, but very few have done it in parents and kids. We’re hoping that it’ll offer another window into what it means to be interacting with another person and offer a new type of insight that we haven’t had before.

There have been a few studies in classrooms where a bunch of students were wearing an EEG cap, as was their teacher. Some students were more in sync with their instructor than others. It’s a pretty new area because collecting EEG on multiple people at a time is even more tricky than collecting EEG on a single child, much less a toddler.

**How tough was it to get an EEG cap on the babies?**

One of the trickiest things that research has been able to do is to try to look at the brains of toddlers because they don’t want to stay still in MRI. It’s hard to get them to do a task like looking at faces even in EEG.

That’s why I’m so excited about this idea of bringing the naturalistic play context into our brain imaging work rather than trying to fit the square peg of toddlers into the round hole of neuroimaging. And actually, what we do, even if we don’t want to look at both the parent and the toddler’s brain together, we put an EEG cap on the parent. When the toddler sees, “Oh, we all wear a funny looking hat when we’re here,” it helps us increase the rate at which we can get toddlers to do a task, even if it’s not a fun and engaging task like the social EEG paradigm. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: After Dinosaurs Died, a Massive Fungus Inherited the Forests
content:
If you spot a mushroom on a hike, there’s a decent chance it’s from an unknown species. The bulk of most fungi exists unseen as vast networks of tiny threadlike mycelia, only popping their fruiting bodies up to spread their spores. In fact, of the estimated 2-6 million species of fungi on Earth, we’ve only identified around 200,000 of them, a tiny fraction. Now there’s one more to add to the list, and it’s a big one.

A team of Chinese mycologists discovered the species after noticing sizable, whitish fruiting bodies near the roots of Chinese cork oak trees located in both subtropical and temperate forests. They appeared to belong to the largest phylum of fungi, ascomycota, which release their spores from sacs rather than producing mushrooms.

**Read more: “[Mushrooms Stole a Trick From Bacteria. It Could Help Us Control the Weather](https://nautil.us/mushrooms-stole-a-trick-from-bacteria-it-could-help-us-control-the-weather-1280034)”**

After collecting samples of the fruiting bodies and hauling them back to the lab, the team cultured their spores, performed genetic analyses, and [published](http://dx.doi.org/10.3389/ffunb.2026.1940464) their findings in _Frontiers in Fungal Biology_. It turns out the fungus wasn’t just a new species (which they called _Dianjunus rex_ in a nod to its king-sized stature), it was unique enough to merit its own new family: dianjunaceae. They determined the family was part of the order xylariales, an ascomycete capable of producing enzymes that break down [lignin](https://nautil.us/did-these-microbes-eat-a-lot-of-the-fossil-record-1285704), the organic polymer that gives wood its sturdy structure.

Comparing _D. rex_’s genome sequence to other fungal species, the team traced its origins to around 65 million years ago. As dinosaur fans will recall, this was a pretty auspicious time period, and it seems that as _T. rex_ fell, _D. rex_ rose. “This timing raises an intriguing possibility,” study author Indunil C. Senanayake of the Kunming Institute of Botany explained in a [statement](https://www.frontiersin.org/news/2026/10/13/frontiers-fungal-biology-giant-fungus-yunnan-dianjunus-rex). “After the mass extinction, forests experienced dramatic changes, including the sudden availability of large amounts of dead plant material. For wood-associated decomposing fungi, such environmental disruption may have created new ecological opportunities.”

According to the team, massive fruiting bodies may have given _D. rex_ an advantage amid the ensuing fungal smorgasbord. “A fruiting body which towers above surrounding vegetation and debris could have better dispersal of spores by wind in dense forests,” Senanayake said. “However, such a large structure requires substantial energy investment, suggesting that this strategy likely evolved only where the ecological benefits outweighed the costs.”

If scientists are only discovering a fungus with giant fruiting bodies now, imagine how many more species are left out there to find. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Was This Neanderthal Murdered?
content:
The Shanidar Cave system in Iraq provided some of the first evidence that Neanderthals, like us, buried their dead. Now, according to a new study [published](http://dx.doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-69193-z) in _Scientific Reports_, it might also be the site of a prehistoric murder mystery.

Within the cave, archaeologists found a scapula (shoulder blade) buried underneath 25 feet of rock belonging to a roughly 45-year-old Neanderthal man who lived around 75,000 years ago called Shanidar A. This flat triangular bone is relatively thin, and Shanidar A’s had a circular hole a little wider than half an inch in his—a puncture wound. Was this murder most foul?

**Read more: “**[**People With This Neanderthal Hormone Receptor Have More Muscle Mass**](https://nautil.us/people-with-this-neanderthal-hormone-receptor-have-more-muscle-mass-1283409)**”**

To find out, the team performed a little high-tech crime scene analysis using computer-generated 3D models of the bone. And they were able to learn quite a bit about what led to Shanidar A’s demise. First, the wound likely resulted from a sharpened wooden spear rather than a stone weapon, which would have left a more angular wound. Neanderthals were [adept woodworkers](https://nautil.us/neanderthals-were-adept-woodworkers-too-1285608), and while most of their handiwork has been lost to time, the round hole is consistent with spear tips unearthed in the United Kingdom. Other Neanderthal spears from Germany seem to have been carefully balanced and optimized for throwing.

Second, beveling on the scapula indicated the killing blow came from the front, and bits of bone point suggest it came from above at a downward trajectory, puncturing the left side. The spear likely pierced the lung and heart. “The position of the wound and the force required to push it right through the Neanderthal’s body bear the hallmarks of an intended kill shot directed towards the heart,” study author Emma Pomeroy of the University of Cambridge said in a [statement](https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/1147227).

So a shot to the heart, but who’s to blame?

This is where things get murky. While the team is confident the killing blow came from another Neanderthal (or even human), they’re not ready to rule it a homicide. It’s possible, researchers say, this was a tragic hunting accident. “Animals such as mammoths may have been hunted up close with thrusting spears, so it’s easy to imagine lethal injuries,” Pomeroy explained.

In other words, this 75,000-year-old cold case will likely go unsolved, but Shanidar A still had more clues to offer about Neanderthal life. The victim’s jaw was also found among his remains and his teeth showed signs of previous trauma. One front incisor had been split in half with the surrounding teeth rotated inward, and tartar buildup indicated the facial drubbing occurred at least a year before Shanidar A was killed.

According to the team, the agonizing injury would have made it difficult for Shanidar A to eat, which means someone likely cared for him. Previous research into the cave found evidence of soaking plants before cooking, and it’s possible this unfortunate Neanderthal benefitted from that food-softening technique.

“The remains of Shanidar A reflect the dual nature of so much of what we recognize as human,” Pomeroy said. “On the one hand, we have evidence of a terribly violent end. On the other, this was clearly an individual who was cared for during their lifetime.”

Just like us, Neanderthals contain multitudes. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)
